name: POPE
description: A polling-based object probing evaluation dataset/pipeline for evaluating object hallucination in large vision-language models, constructed as triples of an image, multiple yes/no questions about objects, and their answers.
creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
citeAs: Li, Yifan; Du, Yifan; Zhou, Kun; Wang, Jinpeng; Zhao, Wayne Xin; Wen, Ji-Rong. Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv:2305.10355v3, 2023.
rai:dataCollection: Given an image caption dataset, POPE constructs a set of triples, each consisting of an image, multiple polling questions, and yes/no answers. Objects in the image are obtained either from human annotations or automatic segmentation tools like SEEM. Questions with answer "Yes" are built from ground-truth objects, while questions with answer "No" are built by sampling nonexistent objects using Random, Popular, or Adversarial sampling strategies. For evaluation on MSCOCO, the authors randomly selected 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects in the annotations and constructed 6 questions for each image; elsewhere they note randomly sampling 2,000 images from the MSCOCO validation set for CHAIR evaluation.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data source is existing image datasets, primarily the validation set of MSCOCO with annotations about contained objects and human-labeled captions. For scalability experiments, images from A-OKVQA and GQA were also annotated using SEEM segmentation results.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors set the ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects as 1:1 for label balance. They formulate each probed object into a question template such as "Is there a/an <object> in the image?" and create evaluation triples. Negative objects are sampled under three settings: Random, Popular, and Adversarial.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For computing CHAIR on MSCOCO, the authors follow prior settings that only consider 80 objects appearing in the MSCOCO segmentation challenge. For POPE on MSCOCO, they randomly select 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects and construct 6 questions per image. For SEEM-based POPE, images are automatically segmented and the resulting object labels are used to build polling questions.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: POPE uses object annotations from existing human annotations or automatic segmentation results from SEEM. Ground-truth objects are used to create positive yes/no questions, and nonexistent objects are sampled to create negative questions. In SEEM-based settings, the tool automatically annotates objects in images. For VQA evaluation, ChatGPT is used to judge whether a model answer matches one of the correct answers.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper analyzes stability by comparing POPE across four prompt templates and reports lower standard deviation than CHAIR. It also analyzes consistency between POPE yes/no responses and generated captions, finding that objects given "No" responses seldom appear in captions and objects mentioned in captions usually receive "Yes" answers. The authors also note divergence between annotation-based and SEEM-based POPE due to finer granularity and label-set inconsistencies.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 6 questions per image on MSCOCO; ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects is 1:1
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that hallucination hinders the safe use of LVLMs in real-world deployment and may result in unexpected consequences caused by hallucinated objects. It gives autonomous driving as an example, where incorrect understanding of the external environment could lead to wrong decisions and serious safety issues. The authors hope the work can help develop more reliable and human-aligned LVLMs.
rai:dataBiases: The authors empirically reveal that object distributions in visual instruction datasets affect hallucination: LVLMs are prone to hallucinate frequently appearing objects and objects that frequently co-occur with ground-truth objects in the image. They also note that visual instruction datasets based on MSCOCO share an unbalanced object distribution where top frequent objects occupy a major part of the dataset.
rai:dataLimitations: The work only focuses on object hallucination and does not measure overall LVLM capability. Due to computation limits, models are evaluated on only part of each validation set, so results may be affected by data distribution. POPE uses a matching-based method to determine whether models answer "Yes" or "No", but models may fail to provide explicit yes/no words, causing inaccurate evaluation. When combined with automatic segmentation, object labels may be inconsistent with human annotations, leading to divergent results. The study also compares only a small number of LVLMs and excludes some recently released or closed-source models.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset/pipeline is intended for evaluation of object hallucination in large vision-language models. It is used to benchmark representative LVLMs on MSCOCO and can be extended to unannotated datasets with automatic segmentation tools such as SEEM. The paper presents it as a more stable, fair, and flexible alternative to instruction-based hallucination evaluation methods like CHAIR.
